title: Chaotic Griffiths phase in neuron map networks
abstract: Griffiths phases provide a mechanism for sustaining critical dynamics over extended parameter regions without fine-tuning to an isolated transition point. This behavior has been mainly associated with structural heterogeneity in complex networks. Here we show that quenched heterogeneity in local parameters can generate a chaotic Griffiths phase in a network of map-based neurons. We study globally coupled Chialvo maps with quenched disorder in a local neuronal parameter, thereby isolating intrinsic parameter disorder from topological disorder. As the coupling strength is varied, a chaotic Griffiths phase emerges between desynchronized and coherent chaotic dynamics, characterized by intermittent formation and breakup of neuronal clusters and large fluctuations in the fraction of clustered neurons. Within this regime, cluster sizes exhibit power-law distributions with coupling-dependent exponents, providing evidence of critical behavior over a finite parameter interval. The chaotic Griffiths phase is absent in the homogeneous limit and broadens progressively as the degree of parameter heterogeneity increases. We further introduce topological disorder through small-world connectivity and find that its combined action with local parameter heterogeneity substantially extends the chaotic Griffiths phase. In both globally coupled and small-world networks, the number of positive Lyapunov exponents displays anomalous scaling with system size. These results demonstrate that intrinsic dynamical heterogeneity constitutes an independent mechanism for generating chaotic Griffiths phases and that its interplay with structural disorder enhances extended criticality in neuronal networks.
summary: This work analyzes chaotic Griffiths phases in coupled neuron networks, demonstrating that local parameter disorder alone can induce extended critical dynamics. The authors show that this intrinsic disorder, when combined with structural disorder like small-world connectivity, significantly broadens the critical regime. The study uses cluster analysis and Lyapunov exponents to confirm that dynamical heterogeneity is a key mechanism for extended criticality.
main_problem: The paper investigates how chaotic Griffiths phases can emerge and be sustained in coupled neuronal networks, specifically differentiating the roles of intrinsic parameter disorder versus structural disorder.
main_result: Intrinsic dynamical heterogeneity alone is sufficient to generate a chaotic Griffiths phase, and combining it with structural disorder (small-world connectivity) significantly extends this critical regime.
method: The study uses time-series analysis, clustering diagnostics (tracking the fraction of clustered neurons, $p_t$), and calculating the dispersion $\sigma(p)$ to characterize the transition between different dynamical regimes.
model_or_system: The model is a network of neurons governed by the Chialvo map, which is coupled either globally or on a Watts-Strogatz small-world topology. Disorder is introduced via quenched randomness in the local neuronal parameters.
key_observables: Fraction of clustered neurons ($p_t$), cluster size distribution exponents ($\alpha$), dispersion of $p_t$ ($\sigma(p)$), and the number of positive Lyapunov exponents ($N_+$).
important_parameters: Coupling strength ($\epsilon$), degree of local parameter heterogeneity ($A$), and the structural disorder parameter (small-world rewiring probability).
main_assumptions: The analysis assumes that the system dynamics can be characterized by the emergence of power-law distributions and anomalous scaling of Lyapunov exponents in the critical regime.
figures_summary: Figures illustrate the time evolution of the clustered fraction ($p_t$) across different regimes (desynchronized, Griffiths, coherent), show power-law scaling of cluster sizes in the Griffiths phase, and demonstrate anomalous scaling of positive Lyapunov exponents ($N_+$) with system size $N$.
paper_structure: The paper first establishes the model using globally coupled neurons with intrinsic disorder, identifying the chaotic Griffiths phase. It then extends the analysis to include small-world connectivity, showing that the combination of both types of disorder broadens the critical regime. Finally, it analyzes the scaling of Lyapunov exponents to confirm the robustness of the critical signatures.
why_interesting: The findings provide a theoretical framework for understanding extended criticality in complex dynamical systems, showing that intrinsic dynamical disorder can mimic or enhance the effects typically associated with structural disorder in network science.
